entries.title: Introducing Geist Serif
entries.summary: Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. entries.content:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Copy link to headingSame system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Copy link to headingDisplay first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

We created something that could only be made for today. Not overly blocky for screens from a decade ago, not filled with mechanical compromises for physical ink. Just serifs at perfect points.Mark Davis founder & font designer at WORDMARK

Copy link to headingFrom the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Copy link to headingGeist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Copy link to headingFour families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Copy link to headingFour variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (

ELSH
), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with 

font-variation-settings
:

Copy link to headingCrafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Copy link to headingSpecs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (

    ss01
    to 
    ss05
    )

  • 352 supported languages

Copy link to headingGetting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

      
npm i geist

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif
    (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif 

  • GeistSerifRegular
    : --font-geist-serif-regular 

  • GeistSerifSquare
    : --font-geist-serif-square 

  • GeistSerifTriangle
    : --font-geist-serif-triangle 

  • GeistSerifHeart
    : --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in 

layout.tsx
with 
GeistSerifRegular
: 
      
import { GeistSerifRegular } from 'geist/font/serif/regular'; 
export default function RootLayout({ children }) {   return (                   {children}       ); }

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

Copy link to headingWhat’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Copy link to headingWeights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Copy link to headingToward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Copy link to headingItalics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

Copy link to headingMore scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

Copy link to headingOne family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

entries.title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
entries.summary: Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service
entries.content:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js 

fetch
caching or 
unstable_cache
, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Copy link to headingWhy we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by 

fetch
caching and 
unstable_cache
. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: 

getCache
from 
@vercel/functions
. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 

'use cache: remote'
, which caches function and component outputs.

Copy link to headingHow Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with 

catalog
. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

Copy link to headingWhat we’ve shipped

Copy link to headingFaster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

Copy link to headingMore storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

Copy link to headingMore visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Copy link to headingBringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js 

fetch
caching and 
unstable_cache
have used Data Cache, while 
getCache
and 
'use cache: remote'
have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use 

fetch
caching or 
unstable_cache
, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

entries.content:
Data Cache is exiting beta and moving to Runtime Cache. Next.js 

fetch
caching and 
unstable_cache
will switch over on every version without code changes. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own Runtime Cache storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Once your team migrates, Data Cache reads and writes that were previously unbilled are charged at Runtime Cache pricing. Rates start at $0.40 per million read units and $4.00 per million write units, and vary by region.

Hobby teams get 1 million read units and 200,000 write units free each month across all projects. On Pro, usage draws from your $20 infrastructure credit each month, and anything beyond it is billed at regional rates. For Enterprise pricing, contact your account team.

Copy link to headingMigration

Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default.

If your team already uses Data Cache:

  • Hobby: We’ll migrate your team on November 29, 2026.

  • Pro: We’ll notify you of your migration date and when billing changes take effect.

  • Enterprise: Your account team will contact you with migration details.

Before you migrate, review your project's Data Cache usage in Observability. To cut unnecessary reads and writes, follow the optimization guide or copy the agent prompt into your coding agent. In the Runtime Cache dashboard, you can also select Optimize with Vercel Agent.

Starting October 30, existing Hobby and Pro teams can opt in early from your team's CDN settings. Runtime Cache pricing applies as soon as you opt in.

You can also disable 

fetch
and 
unstable_cache
caching in CDN settings, which sends more requests to your data sources but doesn’t stop your migration.

Read about the architecture and recent improvements in the blog post.

entries.title: Vercel Daemons can now call services with bindings
entries.summary: Vercel Daemons can now call the services in their deployment through service bindings.Declare the binding on the daemon. It names the target service and the environment variable that receives the service's URL:The daemon calls that URL like any other HTTP endpoint. Vercel handles the internal routing, authentication, and TLS, and the service stays private:Bindings point one way: services can't bin
entries.content:
Vercel Daemons can now call the services in their deployment through service bindings.

Declare the binding on the daemon. It names the target service and the environment variable that receives the service's URL:

vercel.toml

      
[services.api]root = "api/"entrypoint = "main:app"
[daemons.worker]root = "worker/"entrypoint = "Dockerfile"instances = { iad1 = 1 }
[[daemons.worker.bindings]]type = "service"service = "api"format = "url"env = "API_URL"

A daemon binding the api service, exposed to the worker as API_URL

The daemon calls that URL like any other HTTP endpoint. Vercel handles the internal routing, authentication, and TLS, and the service stays private:

worker/worker.ts

      
await fetch(new URL('jobs/next', process.env.API_URL));

Calling the bound service from the daemon with a plain fetch

Bindings point one way: services can't bind to daemons. Each instance keeps calling the deployment that started it, even after a promotion or rollback.

Learn more about daemon service bindings in the docs.

entries.content:
Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 from InclusionAI is now available on AI Gateway, free until November 3, 2026.

The updated model is designed for coding, multi-step reasoning, and agents that use tools. Its 1M-token context window supports workflows involving long documents, code, and extended task histories.

Use 

inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-1019
as the model name: 
      
import { streamText } from 'ai';
const result = streamText({  model: 'inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-1019',  prompt: 'Suggest three ways to make an AI agent more reliable.',});
for await (const text of result.textStream) {  process.stdout.write(text);}

Free requests still appear in your spend dashboard with a full request trace, they just cost nothing. On November 3, requests will begin charging at the published rate.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

      
npx vercel ai-gateway setup

Then select 

inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-1019
in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

You can also try Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

entries.title: Add liveness checks to your Daemons
entries.summary: Vercel Daemons now support configuring HTTP liveness checks.Start with an HTTP endpoint in your daemon that reports its health. Keep it lightweight so it responds quickly, and have it return an error status when the daemon is no longer healthy:The daemon configuration now accepts a livenessProbe value pointing at that endpoint:Vercel periodically requests the endpoint and restarts the daemon's con
entries.content:
Vercel Daemons now support configuring HTTP liveness checks.

Start with an HTTP endpoint in your daemon that reports its health. Keep it lightweight so it responds quickly, and have it return an error status when the daemon is no longer healthy:

      
let alive = true;
startWorker({  onConnectionError: () => { alive = false }})
require('http').createServer((req, res) => {  res.statusCode = alive ? 200 : 500;  res.end();}).listen(1234)

A minimal health endpoint that fails the check when the worker is no longer healthy

The daemon configuration now accepts a 

livenessProbe
value pointing at that endpoint: 
      
{  "daemons": {    "worker": {      "root": "worker/",      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",      "livenessProbe": {        "httpGet": { "port": 1234, "path": "/health" }      }    }  }}

A daemon with an HTTP liveness probe on port 1234

Vercel periodically requests the endpoint and restarts the daemon's container when the check fails, catching a daemon that is still running but no longer healthy.

Read the Daemon documentation for more information about liveness checks, including default values and the optional tuning fields.

entries.title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
entries.summary: IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation hea
entries.content:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the 

geolocation()
helper in 

@vercel/functions
, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.

entries.title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
entries.summary: On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.Faster cold startsTwo changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.Every function invoc
entries.content:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Copy link to headingFaster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Copy link to headingUsage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used 

waitUntil
for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update 

@flags-sdk/vercel
to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application: 
      
pnpm add @flags-sdk/vercel@latest

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

entries.content:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s 

HarnessAgent
now uses 
libfx
, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through 

    toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update 

@ai-sdk/harness-fx
to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.
